summary: The PCE architecture is set out in RFC 4655 and extended in RFC 5623 and RFC 6805, but they leave some questions unanswered, especially about how the architectural views interact. This document discusses those open questions.

eli5.summary: Planning network routes with a helper has some gaps in the rulebook. This RFC lists the questions that the earlier descriptions did not answer.

questions: what are pce architecture open questions
subtitle: Open questions about how networks can plan paths together

tldr.problem: The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture, described in earlier RFCs, was extended for multi-layer networks and hierarchical setups, but left key questions unanswered about how the pieces fit together and interact.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs 26 open questions about PCE and discusses them in an architectural context, referencing protocols and recent IETF work. It does not define answers but suggests how components might be combined.
tldr.outcome: The document serves as a reference for implementers and architects trying to build or deploy PCE-based systems, clarifying what has been left open and what trade-offs exist in different approaches.

today: RFC 7399 remains a reference for PCE architecture questions and considerations. The Stateful PCE extensions mentioned in the RFC were later formalized in draft-ietf-pce-stateful-pce and are being implemented in networks.

sections.title: The PCE Architecture and Its Open Questions
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) is a network component that computes optimal paths for Label Switched Paths (LSPs) through a network. The base PCE architecture was defined in RFC 4655, then extended for multi-layer networks with the Virtual Network Topology Manager (VNTM) in RFC 5623, and generalized to Hierarchical PCE (H-PCE) in RFC 6805. However, these RFCs deliberately left key questions about component interactions unanswered.

This RFC draws out those questions and discusses them in context, referencing existing protocols, IETF work, and deployment scenarios. It suggests how architectural components might be combined but does not define requirements. The document is aimed at implementers and architects who need guidance on real-world PCE deployment.
sections.eli5: PCE helps networks route traffic efficiently, but earlier documents didn't explain how all the pieces work together. This RFC lists the hard questions and thinks through possible answers.

sections.title: Building the Topology Database
sections.content:
A PCE makes decisions based on a Traffic Engineering Database (TED) that holds topology and resource information. The RFC notes that the base architecture does not specify what exact information the TED must contain. At minimum, it must have nodes, links, and connectivity. For most use cases, it also needs link metrics and information about available unallocated resources. Advanced cases may require link delay, jitter, optical impairments, switching capabilities, and Shared Risk Groups.

The RFC raises the question: how is the TED built and maintained? The base architecture suggests feeding it via IGP extensions (OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE). However, running a full IGP at the PCE can be a burden. Alternatives include BGP-LS, which filters and aggregates IGP data through a route reflector, or direct reporting via the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP). In networks without BGP (like some optical networks), the TED may be built from the Network Management System or direct configuration. No single approach works everywhere.
sections.eli5: The PCE needs a map of the network: what links exist, how much space they have, what paths are possible. The question is: where does the PCE get this map? Different networks have different answers.

sections.title: Discovery, Selection, and Hierarchical PCE
sections.content:
A Path Computation Client (PCC) must discover and select a PCE to handle its computation requests. The base architecture allows PCEs to advertise themselves via the IGP, but not all PCEs participate in the IGP. For those cases, other discovery mechanisms like DNS may be needed. When multiple PCEs exist, selection is not trivial: different PCEs may have different capabilities (support for point-to-multipoint computation, specific objective functions, and coverage of different domains). Capabilities can be announced via OSPF/IS-IS flags or PCEP TLVs, but selection is not a negotiation—the PCC must examine advertised capabilities and choose.

For multi-domain networks, Hierarchical PCE introduces parent and child PCEs. The RFC raises questions about parent PCE ownership, discovery (child PCEs must be configured with parent address), authorization, and building a parent domain topology. H-PCE works well for small groups of domains (perhaps up to 20), but scalability limits mean it is not suitable for the Internet as a whole. The number of hierarchy levels is also not constrained, though practical systems rarely exceed two or three.
sections.eli5: A router needs to find a PCE and pick which one to use. With multiple networks involved, a parent PCE coordinates child PCEs in each domain. But how these PCEs find each other and organize is still open.

sections.title: Stateful PCE and Managing LSP State
sections.content:
A Stateless PCE computes paths on demand; it does not remember which LSPs exist in the network. If the PCC wants the PCE to account for other LSPs, it must describe them in the request. A Stateful PCE maintains an LSP database (LSP-DB) of active LSPs in the network, allowing the PCC to refer to LSPs by identifier alone and enabling smarter decisions like balancing LSP distribution or reoptimizing paths.

Building and maintaining the LSP-DB raises challenges. PCCs can report LSP setup and teardown events, but not all LSRs support the PCRpt (PCE Report) message. Some LSPs may traverse only LSRs unaware of the PCE or do not use PCEP. The PCE may need to learn about LSPs through other means: RSVP-TE Record Route information, MIB modules, or NMS integration. For redundant stateful PCEs, keeping their LSP-DBs synchronized is a database synchronization problem with no simple solution.

The RFC also introduces sticky resources: tentative resource reservations made by the PCE after a computation to reduce available resources in the TED, mitigating the risk that another computation uses resources before the first LSP is set up. However, sticky resources introduce complexity: the PCE must track why available resources changed and know when to release sticky resources if LSP setup fails.
sections.eli5: A stateless PCE is like asking for directions each time without memory. A stateful PCE remembers what paths exist and can make smarter decisions. But remembering requires coordination: the PCE must learn about every LSP and stay in sync with other PCEs.

sections.title: Active PCE, Multi-Domain Routing, and Future Extensions
sections.content:
A Passive PCE responds to computation requests but takes no autonomous actions. An Active PCE issues provisioning recommendations: it can suggest new routes for existing LSPs or recommend the instantiation of new ones. An Active PCE needs state to reroute effectively, so it is typically stateful. The distinction matters for deployment: a passive PCE is a decision tool, while an active PCE is a control agent in the network.

The RFC discusses multi-domain path computation methods. The per-domain method has each PCE compute one segment toward the destination without knowing where the destination lies; the Backward Recursive PCE-based Computation (BRPC) seeks a more optimal path but requires knowing the destination domain and the domain sequence. The question of destination discovery in multi-domain networks remains open, with suggestions ranging from IP reachability (via BGP) to GMPLS Calls carrying domain information.

Finally, the RFC hints at advanced topics: how a Virtual Network Topology Manager abstracts multi-layer networks for PCE computation, the role of policy in PCE decisions, and PCE's relationship to Software-Defined Networks (SDN). These areas remain largely unexplored architectural questions.
sections.eli5: A passive PCE suggests paths; an active PCE makes changes. Multi-domain routing requires knowing where the destination is and which domains to cross. Policy and SDN integration are future frontiers.
